evaluation.final_reason: Agent D proposed a concrete adjustment and Agent A accepted it. Agent D: "...on your night, you cook your usual meal, but you also just make a simple side of steamed or boiled vegetables for me?" Agent A: "Yeah, okay. I can do that. Just simple vegetables is fine." Outcome: Agent A will prepare a simple vegetable side on their night; Agent D will prepare their own compliant main and still eat together at 6.30. Agent C maintained their position of not cooking more than one night a week (Turn 5).
Agent B expressed no objection and remained neutral, prioritizing timing (Turn 4).

round_scores.evidence: Agent A asks what's wrong; Agent D reports a medical diet: "The doctor's put me on a really strict diet for the next month. ... I can't eat any meat or anything fried." This creates a new incompatibility with the existing dinner arrangement.

Agent A: "...that's a problem for my night, then. I only cook meat dishes." This expresses a clear, substantive disagreement about how the rota can continue. Agent B's comment that timing is fine does not resolve the core issue.

Agent C: "And I'm not cooking more than one night a week." (refuses extra burden). Agent D proposes a mitigation: "...maybe I can just cook my own meal? I'll still eat with everyone at the same time." The proposal softens the dispute but A has not yet accepted, so substantive disagreement remains.

Agent A: "But the point is we cook for each other. If you're making your own food on my night, we're not really sharing a meal." Agent D: "...the important part is that we're still eating together... It's only for a month." Positions soften but the incompatible expectations about shared cooking persist.

A successful settlement combined small, concrete mutual adjustments: the host adds a simple side while the constrained person prepares their own main.
